fields.current: New state taxes since January 1, 2026 must count under the state spending limit or cannot be collected. The State Auditor reviews programs a proposed special tax would fund before the election, and audits new state special taxes every four years.

evidence.excerpt: The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026, if the state tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds
Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process
This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot
an ongoing financial and performance audit shall be completed every four years

In the event that this initiative measure receives a greater number of affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall prevail in their entirety, and all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void.

fields.explanation: The spending-limit sentence is supported, with 'on or after' rather than 'since'. The pre-election audit applies only to special taxes proposed by citizen initiative, and happens when signatures are being gathered (LAO says at 25 percent), not simply 'before the election'. The four-year audits cover programs funded by special taxes enacted or increased after January 1, 2026. The field omits the conflict clause, which the official summary lists and which is the main way the measure affects Prop 40.
fields.proposedText: New state taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 cannot be excluded from the state spending limit, or the state cannot collect them. The State Auditor reviews programs a special tax proposed by citizen initiative would fund, while signatures are being gathered. It audits programs funded by new state special taxes every four years. If it gets more yes votes than another initiative on this ballot that has a tax excluded from the spending limit, that whole measure is void.
fields.limitations: The 25 percent figure is from LAO. The legal text, as read, ties the trigger to 'a certification for a proposed special tax initiative' submitted to the Secretary of State and does not state 25 percent itself.

conflicts: Prop 40's own conflict clause (Sec. 8) deems in conflict only measures that levy or affect a tax on billionaire net worth or that provide for use of funds from such a tax, and voids only their 'conflicting provisions'. Props 41 and 42 do not levy such a tax on their face. So if Prop 40 outpolls 41 and 42, the text of Prop 40 does not by itself void them. LAist/CalMatters (Sept 24, 2026) says instead: 'If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures.' No official source we read resolves this.
Prop 41 Sec. 5 and Prop 42 Sec. 5 each void 'all the provisions of the other measure' (the whole measure), while Prop 40 Sec. 8 voids only 'any conflicting provisions'. The clauses are asymmetric.

Prop 41's trigger (Sec. 5(a)(1)(B)) is an initiative that 'contains a state tax that is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation'. The Prop 40 official summary says it 'Exempts such tax revenues from ... state spending limit.' That is how Prop 41 reaches Prop 40 without naming it.

Prop 42's trigger (Sec. 5(a)(1)) is an initiative taxing ownership or control of 'retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings', or a tax based on a status present before the measure's effective date. Prop 40 taxes net worth and uses a January 1, 2026 residency date per our Prop 40 entry. Neither Prop 41 nor 42 names Prop 40.

Both Prop 41 and Prop 42 conflict clauses reach only 'another initiative measure'. Prop 43 is a legislative constitutional amendment, so on the text these clauses do not reach it. Neither clause, on its face, makes Props 41 and 42 conflict with each other.
Both Prop 41 Sec. 5(b) and Prop 42 Sec. 5(b) say that if they are superseded by a conflicting measure that is later held invalid, they become 'self-executing and given full force and effect'.

LAO says only that Prop 40 'could be stopped' because 'the courts could find' a conflict. CalMatters (Prop 41 guide) and LAist state it as certain ('Prop. 40 is nullified', 'Prop. 40 is canceled'). Our text correctly follows LAO's hedge.
CalMatters says counting special taxes under the limit could trigger 'automatic refunds'; LAO's Prop 41 analysis does not discuss refunds.
